projects.title: GlanceMap
projects.subtitle: Follow the lesson. Find your place again
projects.description: An AR prototype that keeps the structure of audio lessons visible while you walk.

meta.label: My role

hero.alt: GlanceMap pairs a growing mind map with illustrations while the listener walks.
hero.caption: GlanceMap in use.

sections.title: A mind map that grows with the audio
body: AR glasses could make walks and commutes opportunities for hands-free learning. But learning podcasts demand concentration: listeners check the path, then return to an explanation that has moved on.

Across 14 pilot rounds and a designer workshop, we developed GlanceMap for audio lessons on the go. Its illustrated mind map grows with the narration and keeps earlier ideas visible, so learners can recover how the ideas connect.

In a 16-person study, free recall exceeded our AudioXtend-inspired Illustration Only baseline by 9.6 percentage points immediately and 7.0 percentage points after seven days. Picture recognition was lower—a trade-off between lesson and picture memory.

sections.title: The podcast moves on when attention shifts
body: The podcast keeps playing when attention shifts to the road. Listeners can miss the links between ideas.
Full captions preserve words but compete with watching the path. How can an AR interface help people follow the explanation when they glance back?

figures.alt: Three moments along the walking route, with the crossing and pedestrian signal.
figures.caption: Walk and listen. Check the crossing. Return to the lesson.

items.title: Walk + listen
items.body: “I’m following the explanation.” Ideas arrive in sequence. AR glasses and earbuds deliver a podcast that builds one idea on the next.

items.title: Look away

items.title: Look back

sections.title: 14 rounds, one evolving design

rounds.title: From full captions to keywords
body: Keywords were easier to catch, but learners still had to reconstruct the relationships.

figures.caption: Full captions

tradeoff.con: Too much to read while walking: listeners missed content, and text blocked their view of the path.

figures.caption: Naïve keywords

tradeoff.pro: Keeps key information without blocking the path.
tradeoff.con: Fragmented words were hard to follow or connect into a coherent explanation.

quote.text: “I don’t have time to read such long passages, so I keep missing content. The text blocks my view of the path and traffic lights—it could be unsafe.”

items.title: Insight → short, connected phrases
items.body: Keep text brief. Keep relationships visible.

rounds.title: Replace learned codes with familiar meaning
body: Structured Keywords required learning a visual code. We kept familiar parent–child links and used illustrations for concrete meaning.

figures.caption: Structured keywords

tradeoff.pro: For listeners who understood the layout, the structure was clearer and icons faster to read than words.
tradeoff.con: The workshop’s visual code was not intuitive to everyone; color coding added confusion.

figures.caption: Illustration Only

tradeoff.pro: A state-of-the-art illustrated-audio approach: rich images convey meaning with little reading.
tradeoff.con: Each image explains the current sentence, but gives no overview of the lesson’s logic.

items.title: Insight → familiar structure
items.body: Use parent–child links and pictures for objects and scenes.

quote.text: “I don’t know what the designer means. I would rather read the words—understanding these symbols takes time.”

rounds.title: Keep the big picture, show the current idea
body: Reveal the current branch with the audio; retain earlier branches for returning glances.

figures.caption: Full logic map

tradeoff.pro: Shows the complete logic and relationships between ideas.
tradeoff.con: The map obstructed the path and limited how fast listeners could walk.

figures.caption: Partial logic map

tradeoff.pro: Shows the current branch while keeping the path visible.
tradeoff.con: Learners mainly recalled the current branch; earlier ideas were easily lost without repeated glances back.

figures.alt: Illustration of the gray-past-nodes iteration: earlier branches are gray while the current Distance Cost branch stays green
figures.caption: Gray past nodes

tradeoff.pro: Keeps the path visible and earlier branches available for a glance back.
tradeoff.con: On Quest Pro, gray text was hard to distinguish, so rereading it demanded extra visual effort.

items.title: Insight → reveal, then retain
items.body: Add nodes with the narration. Keep past branches readable.

rounds.colorIteration: Using findings from Icon Colors, we replaced gray with readable grass green for past branches. Bright green marks the current branch, making it easier to find the active topic and distinguish it from earlier ideas.

sections.title: Better lesson recall, poorer picture recognition
body: Free recall improved immediately and after seven days. Perceived lesson structure improved by 1.59 points on a seven-point scale.
Picture recognition fell by 7.1 percentage points: better lesson memory came with poorer picture memory.
No detectable gait difference was found. Workload showed a modest, model-dependent increase.

sections.title: Clear, comfortable, meaningful icons
body: AR glasses could bring directions and messages into everyday life, but color guidance still borrows from phone screens or green-only displays. In full-color optical see-through glasses, real-world light changes how an icon appears: screen contrast alone cannot predict clarity or comfort.

We worked with 8 professional designers and tested 20 participants across three linked studies. We compared color pairs indoors and outdoors, added icon semantics, then tested refinements such as shadows, gradients and outlines.

The result is a set of color guidelines for AR UI designers, supported by systematic experiments. The guidelines connect clarity, comfort and semantics to different uses: noticeable alerts, recognizable controls and quieter persistent status.

The paper §6 reports the refinement study without identifying all eight pilot designers as participants in that later iteration.
Reasoning bridge: paper §5.2 and §6.1, pp.25 and 29: black comfort stability, scene penetration and weaker semantic alignment at hues 240/270 motivate outline/theme-plate and gray variants.

reasoning.title: White symbols: recover the edge
reasoning.observation: White could retain meaning but lose its edge in bright scenes.
reasoning.decision: Test shadows and both nearby-hue gradients.

reasoning.title: Dark symbols: clarify the shape
reasoning.observation: Black felt comfortable, but real-world details could weaken recognition.
reasoning.decision: Move color into the symbol; test outlines and gray backplates.

studyComparisons.result: Clarity improved by 0.88–1.62 points on the 1–5 scale.
Semantics rose from 3.25 to 4.25 / 5; participants also reported stronger attentional draw.
The −30° direction reduced clarity; +30° improved it. At hue135, gradients reduced clarity.
Outlines were described as clear and less intrusive. B20 added little; B30 supported clarity and semantics; B40 caused blending.

sections.title: From interviews to three versions
body: Designers can find traditional color values online, but it is harder to judge their historical fit, trust the reference, or combine them into a complete palette.
We began with ColoGene, connecting color values with their names, origins, periods and meanings. Interviews and the pilot informed Color Atlas; later feedback points toward a future Color Agent.

In the ten-designer pilot, mean self-reported color understanding and decision scores rose by 8.66 points with ColoGene versus 1.21 with usual workflows (five per group). In Atlas feedback, most designers said they would use the system and judged their Atlas-assisted palettes more workable, better justified and more harmonious than those made without it.

sections.title: How designers choose a color
body: We interviewed 12 participants with design backgrounds for 30 to 45 minutes each about finding, comparing and explaining traditional colors.

items.title: Historical fit is hard to judge
items.body: Designers often start by sampling images; P2 used architectural photographs for cultural-heritage projects. These references show how a color looks, but rarely explain its material origins, historical use or symbolism. Designers need this context beside the swatch to judge whether it fits their brief.

items.title: Sources disagree on color values
items.body: Traditional color names do not map to one fixed digital value: the same name can appear as different shades across sources. Keeping the source and historical description beside each value helps designers examine these differences and choose a reference for their intended context.

items.title: A single color does not define a palette
items.body: Participants compared several versions, usually judging appearance and harmony rather than explaining cultural fit. Choosing one traditional color does not reveal which others share the intended setting; designers need a rationale for the whole combination.

quote.text: I usually make several versions and then pick the one that looks best.

sourceRefs: ColoGene paper §4.2, p.4: P2 architectural photographs and P6 choosing among versions; output/color-portfolio/revision-2026-09-29/p3/paper-fulltext.txt:338–344. Initial 12-person formative study, not Atlas interviews.

ColoGene paper §2.2: traditional names need not map to a single fixed digital value; §4.2: reference sampling, aesthetic-led iteration and provenance rarely entering stated rationales. Verified in output/color-portfolio/condensed-paper-evidence.md and paper-evidence.md. No later Atlas interview used as formative evidence.

body: Museum guides may treat a long look as interest, yet viewers can look repeatedly at a detail without using it in their interpretation. We aligned eye movements, later selections and spoken explanations within the same painting region. Repeated returns to some connecting regions suggest a role in navigating the composition—a question for further testing.

figures.alt: Study sequence with original participant photo
figures.sourceOrigin: Gaze paper Figure 2 procedure and Figure 3 native participant-photo crop, page 4.

sections.title: Compare three signals, not gaze alone

figures.alt: High and Low definitions for Gaze, Selection and Language. High Gaze, Low Selection and Low Language are highlighted as HLL.
figures.sourceOrigin: Original paper section 3.3: each signal is independently coded High or Low, yielding eight combinations. Web definitions retain the paper’s coding rule.

sections.title: One region, three different signals
body: HLL appeared in 156 of 1,651 cleaned region records (9.4%), across all 12 analyzed viewers and all 24 paintings. One recorded case shows what the three letters mean together.

figures.alt: The same P16, Hay Wain, A3 record has High Gaze, Low Selection and Low Language codes.

figures.caption: Single-case measurements, compared with the same trial’s region mean
figures.sourceOrigin: Manuscript Figure 5 measurements redrawn in native HTML/CSS; no screenshot table.

dataVisual.title: Many short looks can add up
dataVisual.description: The same A3 record had more visits but shorter individual fixations. High Gaze concerns accumulated time, not how long each look lasted.

figures.alt: Original gaze heatmaps, eye paths and semantic region maps, arranged in three views for the selected painting
figures.sourceOrigin: Paper Figure 3 for original traces; Hay Wain region map uses matching Figure 5 A1–A6 view. Figure 3 historical-scene panel has no verified artwork title, so is described generically.

sections.title: Where mismatches appeared
body: Selected HLL regions linked groups of figures or connected foreground and background. Could repeated looks help viewers navigate a composition? These examples raise that question; they do not establish a cause.

figures.alt: Three original HLL composition examples, with source outlines and lines
figures.sourceOrigin: Gaze paper Figure 4, page 6: three native artwork crops with original annotations retained.

sections.title: Use a mismatch to start a conversation
body: Selected mismatch cases often involved repeated returns, without uniformly prolonged fixations. Several regions connected figures or foreground and background, suggesting that looking can support orientation as well as interpretation.

A museum guide could use a repeatedly viewed region to ask, “What did you notice here?” It could then offer a compositional cue or historical context based on the visitor’s answer. This application follows from the analysis; it was not tested in this study.

sections.title: Make a long painting easier to follow
body: Zooming into a long handscroll can separate a figure from the streets and stories around it.

Guided by 191 survey responses and 30 interviews, we designed ScrollVerse for the eighteenth-century Prosperous Suzhou Scroll: unfolding scenes, social perspectives and visual inquiry support contextual exploration.

In a 60-person comparison using the same painting and cultural content, 25 of 30 ScrollVerse users reported clearer understanding of Qing-dynasty urban life. The study found no clear difference in usability or workload between the interfaces.

projects.title: VerseColor
projects.subtitle: Follow a color into a poem
projects.description: A visual reading tool for interpreting color in Chinese poetry, with associations that readers can check against the poems.
projects.meta: iConference · Under review · Sep 2026 · corresponding author

hero.alt: A network of colored bubbles connecting poetic colors, imagery and emotion.

sections.title: From finding poems to understanding their imagery
body: A color word can carry different meanings across poems. Eight reader interviews showed that keyword search finds occurrences but leaves readers to assemble their cultural and emotional associations.
VerseColor brings those associations into one visual reading space. Eight expert reviewers checked proposed links against the source texts.

In a 30-person comparison with a widely used Chinese poetry search website, readers rated VerseColor more helpful for connecting ideas and interpreting imagery. The poetry website was easier to use, making navigation the next design priority.

sections.title: A meal is never just a meal
body: Good food is a luxury, and Lufa is a new Deliciousness Insurance salesperson who finishes his first week without a sale. Business dinners offer access to potential clients—but draw him into their expectations and favors.

We use Chinese dining culture to explore the pressure hidden in a shared meal: whom do you accommodate, and at what cost? Conversations and table puzzles turn the familiar promise of ‘for your own good’ into choices about belonging and self-direction.

projects.subtitle: Who gets to tell her story?
projects.description: Rebuild Shangguan Waner and Princess Taiping’s memories across six chapters. Assemble their scenes, watch them dissolve into accusations, then restore their agency—a narrative puzzle about who tells women’s history.

sections.title: Two lives beyond scandal
body: Shangguan Waner wrote imperial edicts in Tang-dynasty China; Princess Taiping shaped court politics. The discovery of Waner’s epitaph in 2013 prompted us to revisit stories of scandal and rivalry.
We made this game to ask how those stories obscure women’s work, friendships and political agency.

role.label: My role
role.details: I independently researched the cases, created the portraits, and designed and built the interactive archive.

projects.revision: 2026-10-16 · Unified archive abstract, solo authorship and remembrance invitation
sourceNotes: 2026-10-16: Author confirmed solo project, 191 documented cases and full archive range 1826–2026. Selected timeline remains ten cases spanning 1826–2016. Archive categories are grounded in the existing case records. Portraits retain the project’s AI-assisted provenance disclosure.
2026-10-16: User confirms reliable news + direct human harm as inclusion criteria; cases are distinct events, not merged reports; indirect-impact extinction cases excluded.

16 October 2026 independent comprehension check: ten selected cases include individuals, pairs and groups; dates label the event rather than necessarily death. Great auk date kept at 1844 to avoid false month precision. Ming wording narrowed to research collection/analysis; age 507 and climate-record context follow linked Bangor University article (14 November 2013). No reason inferred for any of the 95 unpublished research records.
